American [[Jazz|jazz]] trumpeter, cornetist, and singer, nicknamed "Satchmo" and "Pops." Born and raised in [[New Orleans]], he came to prominence in the 1920s as an inventive trumpet and cornet player and became a foundational influence in jazz, shifting the music's focus from collective improvisation to solo performance. Around 1922 he followed his mentor, Joe "King" Oliver, to Chicago to play in Oliver's Creole Jazz Band. His reputation at "cutting contests" reached bandleader Fletcher Henderson, and he moved to New York City, where he became a featured soloist and recording artist. By the 1950s he was an international musical icon.

His best-known songs include "What a Wonderful World," "La Vie en rose," "Hello, Dolly!," "On the Sunny Side of the Street," and "When the Saints Go Marching In." He made three records with [[Ella Fitzgerald]]: *Ella and Louis* (1956), *Ella and Louis Again* (1957), and *Porgy and Bess* (1959). He won the Grammy Award for Best Male Vocal Performance for "Hello, Dolly!" in 1965 and a posthumous Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 1972, and was inducted into the DownBeat Jazz Hall of Fame and the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]].

His gravelly voice and skill at scat singing made him an influential vocalist, and his influence reached popular music. He was one of the first popular African American entertainers to "cross over" to white and international audiences. He rarely discussed racial issues publicly, sometimes to the dismay of fellow black Americans, but took a well-publicized stand for desegregation in the Little Rock Crisis. His recording of "Melancholy Blues" is included on the [[Voyager Golden Record]].

French chemist, pharmacist, and microbiologist, renowned for his discoveries of the principles of [[Vaccination|vaccination]], microbial [[Fermentation|fermentation]], and [[Pasteurization|pasteurization]], which was named after him. He is regarded as one of the founders of modern bacteriology and has been called the "father of bacteriology" and the "father of microbiology," the latter title shared with [[Robert Koch]] and also attributed to [[Antonie van Leeuwenhoek]]. His work is credited with saving millions of lives through vaccines for [[Rabies|rabies]] and [[Anthrax|anthrax]].

Born in Dole, Jura, to a poor tanner's family, he was an average student whose early interests were fishing and sketching. He became professor of chemistry at the University of Strasbourg, where he married Marie Laurent in 1849.

In chemistry, his investigation of sodium ammonium tartrate initiated the field of optical isomerism, and he explained the molecular basis of the asymmetry of certain [[Crystal|crystals]]. He disproved spontaneous generation by showing that nothing developed in sterilized, sealed flasks, while microorganisms grew in sterilized but open ones; the French Academy of Sciences awarded him the Alhumbert Prize of 2,500 francs in 1862. His experiments supported the germ theory of disease by showing that diseases could be prevented by killing or stopping germs, and he developed the treatment of milk and wine to stop bacterial contamination. He developed vaccines for anthrax in cattle and sheep (1881) and for rabies (1885), the latter first given to Joseph Meister, a boy bitten by a rabid dog.

He directed the Pasteur Institute, established in 1887, until his death and was interred in a vault beneath it. His reputation became associated with controversies; a historical reassessment of his notebook revealed that he practiced deception to overcome his rivals.

Range of strong, positive emotional and mental states, from the most sublime virtue to the deepest interpersonal affection to the simplest pleasure. A mother's love differs from a spouse's, which differs from love of food; most commonly the word refers to a feeling of strong attraction and emotional attachment. Many languages use several words for what English calls love, and cultural differences make a universal definition difficult.

Love is considered both positive and negative. Its virtue represents human kindness, compassion, and affection ("the unselfish, loyal and benevolent concern for the good of another"), while its vice is a moral flaw akin to vanity, selfishness, and egotism, potentially leading to [[Mania|mania]], obsessiveness, or codependency. It is commonly contrasted with hate and with [[Lust|lust]], facilitates interpersonal relationships, and is one of the most common themes in the creative arts.

Ancient Greek philosophers identified six forms: familial love (*storge*), friendly or platonic love (*philia*), romantic love (*eros*), self-love (*philautia*), guest love (*xenia*), and divine or unconditional love (*agape*). The triangular theory holds that intimacy, passion, and commitment are love's core components. Some historians date modern conceptions of romantic love to courtly Europe during or after the [[Middle Ages]], though ancient love poetry attests earlier romantic attachments.

Philosophers have offered competing definitions. [[Thomas Aquinas]], following [[Aristotle]], defined love as "to will the good of another," and [[Bertrand Russell]] described it as a condition of "absolute value." Neurobiological accounts instead describe romantic love as driven by hormones such as [[Oxytocin|oxytocin]], vasopressin, and [[Dopamine|dopamine]] in phases of lust, attraction, and attachment, and as an adaptation promoting pair-bonding, parental care, and cooperation.

German composer and pianist, a seminal figure in the [[History of music|history of music]] whose personal style was a key driver of the transition from Classical to Romantic music. He expanded instrumental forms such as the [[Symphony|symphony]], the piano [[Sonata|sonata]], and the string quartet, and his compositions are among the most performed in the world.

Born in [[Bonn]], he was a musical prodigy, taught intensively by his father, Johann van Beethoven, and later by Christian Gottlob Neefe. At 21 he moved to [[Vienna]], which became his base, and studied composition with [[Joseph Haydn]]. He gained a reputation as a virtuoso pianist, and his three Piano Trios, Op. 1 (1795), were the earliest works to which he gave an opus number. Around 1798 he began experiencing symptoms of hearing loss, which he described in the Heiligenstadt Testament of 1802; by 1815 he had ceased public performances.

His career is divided into three periods. In the first he composed in the style of Haydn and [[Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart]]; his First Symphony premiered in 1800. In the middle period (1802–1812) he developed a distinctive style: the Third (*Eroica*) and Fifth Symphonies premiered in 1805 and 1808, the former unprecedented in scale and scope, and his opera *Fidelio* in 1805. The late period (1812–1827) included the *Missa solemnis* and the Ninth Symphony, both premiered in 1824, the latter the first major example of a choral symphony. The *Diabelli* Variations, the *Hammerklavier* sonata, and the late string quartets, including the *Große Fuge*, are regarded as summits of their genres. His output includes nine symphonies, 32 piano sonatas, 16 string quartets, and five piano concertos.

Primary respiratory organ of many animals, including humans. In mammals and most other [[Tetrapod|tetrapods]], two lungs lie near the backbone on either side of the heart. Their function is gas exchange: they extract [[Oxygen|oxygen]] from the atmosphere into the bloodstream and release [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]] from the blood. In early tetrapods, pharyngeal muscles drove air into the lungs by buccal pumping, a mechanism still seen in amphibians; in humans the primary breathing muscle is the diaphragm. The lungs also provide the airflow that makes vocalization, including speech, possible.

Human lungs sit in the thoracic cavity. The right lung is bigger and heavier than the left, which shares space with the heart and has an indentation, the cardiac notch, to accommodate it. The right has three lobes and the left two. Together the lungs weigh approximately 1.3 kg and contain approximately 2,400 km of airways and 300 to 500 million alveoli. Air passes from the trachea into bronchi and bronchioles, which divide until it reaches the microscopic alveoli, where gas exchange takes place. Each lung is enclosed in a pleural sac of two pleurae that slide over each other with little friction during breathing. The blood supply is unusual: deoxygenated blood arrives from the heart through the pulmonary circulation, while a separate bronchial circulation supplies oxygenated blood.

Lung tissue can be affected by diseases such as [[Pneumonia|pneumonia]] and [[Lung cancer]]. Chronic conditions such as [[Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease]] and emphysema can be related to [[Smoking|smoking]] or exposure to harmful substances.

In embryonic development the lungs begin as an outpouching of the foregut. The [[Fetus|fetus]] does not breathe, and blood is diverted from the lungs through the ductus arteriosus. At birth air begins to pass through the lungs and the duct closes.

Thermodynamic system that uses power to apply forces and control movement to perform an action. The term is commonly applied to artificial devices, such as those employing engines or motors, but also to natural biological macromolecules, called molecular machines. Machines can be driven by animal and human power, by natural forces such as wind and water, and by chemical, thermal, or electrical power, and include a system of mechanisms that shape the actuator input to achieve a specific output of force and movement. They can also include computers and sensors that monitor performance and plan movement. Modern machines are complex systems of structural elements, mechanisms, and control components with interfaces for convenient use; examples include trains, automobiles, boats, airplanes, home and office appliances, farm machinery, machine tools, factory automation systems, and robots.

The English word comes through Middle French from Latin *machina*, itself from Greek *mekhane* ("contrivance, machine, engine"). The modern meaning developed from its use for stage engines in theater and for military siege engines in the late 16th and early 17th centuries.

The elementary devices from which machines are built are the six classic [[Simple machine|simple machines]]: wedge, inclined plane, wheel and axle, lever, pulley, and screw. Renaissance natural philosophers identified them and calculated the ratio of output force to input force, known as mechanical advantage. The wedge, exemplified by the flint hand axe, is the oldest, followed by the inclined plane, used since prehistoric times to move heavy objects. The other four were invented in the ancient Near East: the wheel and axle in [[Mesopotamia]] in the 5th millennium BC, the lever about 5,000 years ago, the pulley in the early 2nd millennium BC, and the screw, the last, during the Neo-Assyrian period (911–609 BC).

[[Archimedes]] studied the lever, pulley, and screw around the 3rd century BC and discovered the principle of mechanical advantage in the lever. [[Hero of Alexandria]] (c. 10–75 AD) described five mechanisms that can "set a load in motion," though Greek understanding was limited to statics and did not include dynamics or the concept of work. Windmills and wind pumps appeared in the Muslim world by the 9th century AD, and Al-Jazari described programmable automata in 1206. In 1586 Simon Stevin derived the mechanical advantage of the inclined plane, and [[Galileo Galilei]] worked out the complete dynamic theory of simple machines in 1600, recognizing that they transform energy rather than create it. The classic rules of sliding friction were discovered by [[Leonardo da Vinci]], rediscovered by Guillaume Amontons (1699), and developed by Charles-Augustin de Coulomb (1785).

[[James Watt]] patented his parallel motion linkage in 1782, making the double-acting steam engine practical. Steam engines powered locomotives, steamships, and factories during the [[Industrial Revolution]] (1750–1850), which began with the mechanization of the textile industry in Great Britain.

Branch of [[Economics|economics]] concerned with the performance, structure, behavior, and decision-making of an economy as a whole, whether regional, national, or global. Macroeconomists study aggregate measures such as output or [[Gross domestic product|gross domestic product]] (GDP), national income, [[Unemployment|unemployment]], [[Inflation|inflation]], consumption, saving, investment, and trade; the three central variables are output, unemployment, and inflation.

Macroeconomics and [[Microeconomics|microeconomics]] are the two most general fields of economics. Microeconomists study markets and decision-making at a smaller level, such as firms or consumers, and the divide is institutionalized because of differences in methods and outcomes of interest. Macroeconomics is further divided by time frame. The short run (a few years) concerns business-cycle fluctuations and changes in aggregate demand, which stabilization policies such as monetary and fiscal policy aim to address. In the medium run (about a decade), output tends toward a level set by supply factors such as capital stock, technology, and labor force, and unemployment reverts to its structural, or "natural," level. The long run (a couple of decades or more) emphasizes the determinants of [[Economic growth|economic growth]].

As a separate field, macroeconomics is generally recognized to have begun in 1936, when [[John Maynard Keynes]] published *The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money*, though its intellectual predecessors are older. Swedish economist Knut Wicksell's *Interest and Prices* (1898, translated into English in 1936) is considered pioneering, while Keynes, who introduced national income accounting and related concepts, is called the founding father of the formal discipline. Since [[World War II]], Keynesian, monetarist, new classical, and new Keynesian economists have contributed to mainstream research. Critics argue that reliance on aggregate assumptions can overlook microeconomic foundations and that empirical tests reveal limits in predictive accuracy.

Class of physical phenomena arising through a [[Magnetic field|magnetic field]], which allows objects to attract or repel each other. Because both electric currents and the magnetic moments of elementary particles give rise to a magnetic field, magnetism is one of two aspects of [[Electromagnetism|electromagnetism]]. The familiar effects occur in [[Ferromagnetism|ferromagnetic]] materials, which are strongly attracted by magnetic fields and can be magnetized to become permanent magnets. Only a few substances are ferromagnetic; the most common are [[Iron|iron]], cobalt, nickel, and their alloys.

All substances exhibit some type of magnetism, and materials are classified by bulk susceptibility. Paramagnetic substances, such as aluminium and oxygen, are weakly attracted to an applied field; diamagnetic substances, such as copper and carbon, are weakly repelled; antiferromagnetic materials, such as chromium, have a more complex relationship with a field.

Magnetism was first noticed in the ancient world when lodestones, naturally magnetized pieces of the mineral magnetite, were seen to attract iron. The word *magnet* comes from the Greek for "the Magnesian stone." Aristotle attributed the first scientific discussion of magnetism to [[Thales of Miletus]]. The earliest Chinese literary reference is in the 4th-century BC book *Guiguzi*, and the 11th-century scientist [[Shen Kuo]] was the first to write of the magnetic needle compass, in the *Dream Pool Essays*. By the 12th century the Chinese used the lodestone compass for navigation. In 1600 [[William Gilbert (physicist)|William Gilbert]] concluded from experiments with a model earth that the Earth is itself magnetic, which explains why compasses point north. Understanding of the relationship between electricity and magnetism began when [[Hans Christian Ørsted]] discovered that an electric current could create a magnetic field.

Indian lawyer, anti-colonial nationalist, and political ethicist who used nonviolent resistance to lead the campaign for India's independence from British rule. The honorific Mahatma ("great-souled"), first applied to him in 1914 in South Africa, is now used throughout the world.

Born and raised in a Hindu family in coastal [[Gujarat]], he trained in law at the Inner Temple in London and was called to the bar at 22. Unable to build a successful practice in India, he moved to South Africa in 1893 to represent an Indian merchant in a lawsuit and lived there for 21 years. There he raised a family and first employed nonviolent resistance in a civil rights campaign. In 1915, aged 45, he returned to India and began organizing peasants, farmers, and urban laborers to protest discrimination and excessive land tax.

Assuming leadership of the [[Indian National Congress]] in 1921, he led nationwide campaigns for easing poverty, expanding women's rights, building religious and ethnic amity, ending untouchability, and above all achieving *swaraj*, or self-rule. He undertook long fasts as a means of introspection and political protest. He led the 400 km Dandi Salt March against the British-imposed salt tax in 1930 and called on the British to quit India in 1942, and was imprisoned many times.

His vision of an independent India based on religious pluralism was challenged in the early 1940s by a Muslim nationalism demanding a separate homeland. In August 1947 Britain granted independence and partitioned British India into a Hindu-majority India and a Muslim-majority Pakistan. Religious violence broke out, especially in Punjab and Bengal. Gandhi visited affected areas and undertook several hunger strikes, the last begun in Delhi on January 12, 1948. Nathuram Godse, a militant Hindu nationalist from [[Pune]], assassinated him at an interfaith prayer meeting in Delhi. He is considered the Father of the Nation in India.

Largest branch of [[Buddhism]], followed by the older [[Theravada]]. Its name is Sanskrit for "Great Vehicle." It is a broad group of Buddhist traditions, texts, philosophies, and practices that developed in ancient India from about the 1st century BC onward. It accepts the main scriptures and teachings of early Buddhism but also recognizes scriptures that Theravada does not accept as canonical. Scriptures such as the Lotus Sutra and the Vajra-cutter Sutra emphasize the ideal of the *bodhisattva*, who vows to attain buddhahood to save all living beings, a compassionate attitude called *bodhicitta*.

Mahayana generally holds that buddhahood through the bodhisattva path is available to all beings who take the bodhisattva vow, and it regards the state of the arhat as incomplete and a lesser aspiration. Its buddhology includes buddhas and bodhisattvas absent from Theravada, such as Amitabha and Vairocana, and distinctive conceptions of buddhahood such as *Trikaya* and *Upaya*. Its philosophy includes the Madhyamaka theory of emptiness (*sunyata*) and the idealistic Vijnanavada, the "doctrine of consciousness."

Initially a small movement in India, Mahayana became an influential force in Indian Buddhism, and large scholastic centers associated with it, such as Nalanda and Vikramashila, thrived between the 7th and 12th centuries. It spread from South Asia to Central Asia, East Asia, Southeast Asia, and the Himalayan regions. Traditions such as [[Zen]], Pure Land, and Tiantai are the predominant forms of Buddhism in China, Korea, Japan, Taiwan, Singapore, Vietnam, the Philippines, Malaysia, and Indonesia. [[Vajrayana]], or Mantra traditions, a subset of Mahayana using tantric methods considered to lead swiftly to buddhahood, are dominant in [[Tibet]], Mongolia, Bhutan, and other Himalayan regions. As of 2010, 53% of Buddhists belonged to East Asian Mahayana and 6% to Vajrayana, compared with 36% to Theravada.
